summary: Defines a data model and a JSON representation for contact cards, for storing and exchanging address book data. It is intended as an alternative to vCard that is unambiguous, extendable, and simple to process. Unlike the earlier jCard format, it is not a direct mapping of vCard and adds meaning where appropriate.

eli5.summary: A contact card holds a person's name, phone, and address. This is a tidy way to write those cards in a format computers and programmers find easy to read.

questions: what is the jscontact media type
subtitle: A JSON data model for address-book cards, built as a cleaner alternative to vCard.

tldr.problem: vCard is the standard interchange format for contacts, but it has gone through several versions, only a subset of the old version 3 is widely used, and services often fall back on proprietary JSON in their APIs.
tldr.mechanism: JSContact defines a Card object made of simple key-value properties, written as I-JSON. Properties are typed, extensible through registries and vendor prefixes, and can be localized with patches.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9553 is a Proposed Standard. It gives address book and directory applications a standard JSON alternative to vCard, and two companion documents cover new vCard elements and conversion.

today: RFC 9553 is a Proposed Standard. It is not obsoleted or updated by another RFC in the unit metadata. It works together with RFC 9554 and RFC 9555.

sections.title: Why a New Contact Format
sections.content:
RFC 9553 defines JSContact, a data model and JSON representation for the contact cards used in address book and directory applications. It aims to be an alternative to the vCard format from RFC 6350.

The RFC explains the motivation. vCard went through several iterations, and only a subset of its deprecated version 3 is widely used. Products therefore keep an internal contact model that is richer than what they expose in vCard, and service providers often use a proprietary JSON form in their APIs. Missing features such as social media contacts and gender pronouns also showed that vCard was not seen as an evolving format.

The design goals are listed plainly: stay mostly compatible with the vCard model while adding attributes where appropriate, describe card data as simple key-value pairs, avoid ambiguity, and ensure that extensions MUST NOT require an update of this document. Unlike the JSON-based jCard format (RFC 7095), JSContact is not a direct mapping of the vCard model.

Two companion documents complete the picture: RFC 9554 defines new vCard properties and parameters, and RFC 9555 defines how to convert JSContact data from and to vCard.
sections.eli5: The old way of writing contact cards had gotten messy, like a recipe book with many edits. JSContact starts a clean, simple page that computers can read easily.

sections.title: Objects, Types and Patches
sections.content:
JSContact data is JSON, and it MUST be valid I-JSON (RFC 7493), a strict subset of JSON (RFC 8259). A JSContact object is a JSON object with a type name registered at IANA, a set of named properties, and an @type property naming its type. Property names, type names and enumerated values are case-sensitive.

The @type property is often implied by where an object sits. It MAY be set when the property definition already implies the type, but the topmost object in the data MUST set it.

The RFC also defines common data types:

  • Id: a string of 1 to 255 octets using only the base64url alphabet without padding (letters, digits, hyphen and underscore). Many properties are maps from an Id to an object, which acts as an unordered set whose entries each have a stable name.
  • Int and UnsignedInt: integers within the safe range of a double-precision number, up to 2^53-1.
  • UTCDateTime: an RFC 3339 date-time with uppercase letters and the offset Z. Fractional seconds appear only when non-zero and never with trailing zeros, so each instant has a single representation. For example, 2010-10-10T10:10:10.000Z is invalid.
  • PatchObject: a map of paths to new values, using a subset of JSON Pointer (RFC 6901). A null value removes a property. Implementations MUST reject a PatchObject in its entirety if any patch is invalid and MUST NOT apply partial patches.

Patches cannot insert into or delete from an array. To add or remove array members, replace the complete array.
sections.eli5: Every piece of a card has a label saying what kind of thing it is, like name tags at a party. A patch is a sticky note saying 'change just this one line' instead of rewriting the whole card.

sections.title: The Card Object
sections.content:
The top-level object is the Card. It stores information about a person, organization or company. Only two properties are mandatory: version (the JSContact version, such as 1.0) and uid, an identifier that ties the card together across systems. The uid SHOULD be a URN, preferably in the uuid namespace, with UUID version 4 RECOMMENDED.

Other metadata properties include created and updated (both UTCDateTime), prodId (the product that created the card), language (an RFC 5646 tag) and relatedTo, a map from the uid of another card to a relation such as friend, colleague or spouse.

The kind property says what the card represents. It defaults to individual and can also be group, org, location, device or application. A members property, whose keys are the uid values of member cards, MUST only be used when kind is group.

The rest of the card is grouped by purpose: name and organization, contact, calendaring and scheduling, address and location, resources, multilingual, and additional properties.
sections.eli5: A Card is like an index card with a unique ID number on it. The ID lets different address books know they are talking about the same person.

sections.title: Names, Contact Details and Other Properties
sections.content:
The name property holds a Name object. Its components list contains name parts, each with a value and a kind, so a single value can have several words, such as the surname van Gogh. If the components are in a sensible order, isOrdered MUST be true, and separator components or a defaultSeparator say what to put between them. A full string is allowed, and MUST be set when there are no components. A sortAs map says how to sort by each kind of component.

Contact details are maps from an Id to a small object:

  • emails: each has a mandatory address, which MUST be an addr-spec from RFC 5322.
  • phones: each has a mandatory number, either a URI such as a tel URI or free text, and optional features such as mobile, voice, text, video, fax or pager.
  • onlineServices, nicknames, organizations, titles, preferredLanguages, addresses, calendars, schedulingAddresses, cryptoKeys, directories, links and media.

Several of these share common properties. contexts marks where information applies (private or work, and for addresses also billing or delivery). pref ranks entries from 1 to 100, where 1 is most preferred and no value means least preferred. A label carries a custom text label.

Newer needs are covered too: speakToAs records a grammatical gender and chosen pronouns, and anniversaries records birth, death or wedding dates, which can be partial dates such as only a month and day. The phonetic properties, with phoneticSystem values ipa, jyut or piny, say how to pronounce a value.
sections.eli5: Each card has labelled boxes: one for the name, one for phone numbers, one for emails. Each phone number can say 'work' or 'home', and you can mark your favorite with a 1.

sections.title: Localizing a Card
sections.content:
The localizations property lets one card carry the same information in several languages. Its keys are language tags and its values are PatchObjects. Localizations provide alternatives for existing values and SHOULD NOT add new properties, and a patch MUST NOT target the localizations property itself.

The RFC describes the procedure conceptually. To localize a card, find the entry for the wanted language tag (if there is none, stop), copy the card without its localizations property, apply all the patches to the copy, optionally set language, and use the result as the localized variant.

The patch paths can reach deep. In the RFC's example, the path titles/t1/name replaces only the title name with a Spanish word while leaving everything else untouched. Another example replaces a whole name with Ukrainian text in Cyrillic script, and one adds Cantonese Jyutping pronunciations to a Chinese name.
sections.eli5: It is like a card with sticky notes in other languages. If you speak Spanish, you peel on the Spanish sticky note and read that line instead.

sections.title: Validation, Extensions and Versions
sections.content:
A JSContact object is invalid if any of its properties is invalid. Implementations MUST validate and reject invalid IANA-registered properties. Properties they do not recognize but whose names are syntactically valid MUST NOT be treated as invalid. They MUST be preserved, so that systems implementing different extensions can interoperate without data loss. The RFC reserves one property name, extra, which never occurs in any object and can be used by implementations to hold unknown data.

Vendors can add their own properties for experimentation or single-product data. A vendor-specific name MUST start with a prefix that is a domain name under the setter's control, followed by a colon and a name, such as example.com:foo. The prefix ietf.org and its subdomains are reserved for IETF specifications. Vendors who want interoperation are strongly encouraged to register properties, types and values at IANA instead.

Every card states its JSContact version in its version property, and the media type has a matching version parameter. A version has a major and a minor number. A major change signals backwards-incompatible differences, while a minor change only adds things, and a new minor version MUST NOT require implementations to change how they process data. This RFC registers version 1.0.
sections.eli5: If you find a note on a card in a code you do not know, you leave it there instead of throwing it away. That way the next person who knows the code can still read it.

sections.title: IANA Registries and Media Type
sections.content:
RFC 9553 registers the media type application/jscontact+json, with an optional version parameter that MUST NOT occur more than once. If it is set, all JSContact version properties in the body MUST match it. The encoding considerations are the same as for application/json, and applications that currently use the text/vcard media type can use this one as an alternative.

IANA has also created a JSContact registry group with four registries: the JSContact Version registry, the JSContact Properties registry, the JSContact Types registry and the JSContact Enum Values registry. The properties, object types and enumerated values defined in the RFC are all registered there. The registry procedure involves preliminary community review, a request to IANA and designated expert review.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps a public notebook of every official card property name, so two people never invent the same word with different meanings.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC stresses that contact information is very privacy sensitive. It can reveal identity, location, credentials, employment status, interests and social network, so transmission and storage must be done carefully. A malicious actor might also supply a card that uses one person's name with the attacker's contact details, so systems must authenticate the data they receive. The RFC notes that it only defines the data format, and these concerns mainly belong to the API or storage method.

For JSON parsing, the security considerations of RFC 8259 apply. Parsers must check syntax thoroughly, stop at the end of data when scanning for closing brackets, and handle escape sequences carefully. Implementations may want to limit allocation sizes.

Many properties hold URIs, which need extra care. Fetching remote resources reveals IP address information, and should be limited to allowed protocols and well-known ports (generally HTTP and HTTPS on their default ports), without access to internal resources. A malicious card with a very large number of URIs could be an amplification vector for denial of service, so automatic fetching of linked resources should be limited.
sections.eli5: A contact card tells a lot about you, so keep it safe. Also do not blindly follow every link on a card you got from a stranger.

items.label: title
items.desc: An honorific title or prefix, such as Mr., Ms. or Dr.

items.label: given
items.desc: A given name, also known as first name or personal name.

items.label: given2
items.desc: A name between the given name and surname, such as a middle or patronymic name.

items.label: surname
items.desc: A surname, also known as last name or family name.

items.label: surname2
items.desc: A secondary surname used in some cultures.

items.label: credential
items.desc: A credential or honorific suffix, such as B.A. or Esq.

items.label: generation
items.desc: A generation marker, such as Jr. or III.

items.label: separator
items.desc: A verbatim formatting separator between two ordered components.
